content: The ampere, commonly referred to as the amp (symbol: A), is the unit of electric current, which quantifies the amount of electric charge passing a point per second. It is one of the seven base units in the International System of Units (SI) and is named after André-Marie Ampère, a key figure in the discovery of electromagnetism. The ampere is defined as the constant current that, if maintained in two straight, parallel conductors of infinite length, with negligible circular cross-section, and placed one meter apart in a vacuum, would generate a force of 2 × 10⁻⁷ newtons per meter of length between the conductors. This definition is rooted in Ampère's force law, which describes the interaction between electric currents. The ampere is a fundamental unit and is defined independently of the concept of electric charge. Instead, the unit of charge, the coulomb, is derived from the ampere, being the amount of charge transported by a one-ampere current in one second. Conversely, one ampere corresponds to the flow of one coulomb of charge per second. Mathematically, the relationship between charge (Q), current (I), and time (t) is expressed as Q = I × t. The volt and the ohm are tied to reproducible physical phenomena: the Josephson junction for voltage and the quantum Hall effect for resistance. The official realization of the ampere is detailed in the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publication 330. The ampere can also be described in terms of elementary charges. Since one coulomb is approximately equal to 6.24150948 × 10¹⁸ elementary charges (such as electrons), one ampere corresponds to the flow of this number of charges per second. Proposals have been made to redefine the ampere and other SI base units in terms of fixed values of fundamental constants. For example, one proposed definition of the kilogram involves the force generated between two parallel conductors carrying a current of exactly 6.241509479607717888 × 10¹⁸ elementary charges per second. This redefinition would fix the value of the elementary charge (e) to 1.60217653 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs, resulting in a consistent and functionally equivalent definition of the ampere. In 2005, the CIPM approved, in principle, the development of new definitions and practical realizations of these units. Additionally, the CIPM considered redefining the mole in terms of a fixed value of the Avogadro constant and prepared a draft resolution to inform Member States of these activities at the 23rd CGPM in 2007.
